journal_name: ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems

abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel theoretical framework that reformulates the VLSI placement problem as a Markov decision process, fundamentally departing from traditional combinatorial optimization approaches. In conventional electronic design automation, placement algorithms rely predominantly on deterministic cost functions and gradient-based or heuristic search techniques. Our framework introduces reinforcement learning with graph neural networks to enable autonomous exploration of the physical design space, where the agent learns optimal placement policies through environmental interaction. The theoretical contributions include formal proofs of convergence for the proposed policy gradient method under non-convex layout constraints, along with a comprehensive analysis of the state-action space representation using hypergraph embeddings. We establish that the learned placement policy achieves sub-linear regret bounds with respect to wirelength optimization. Experimental validation conducted on ISCAS-85 and ITC-99 benchmark circuits demonstrates that the proposed paradigm yields a 23% improvement in half-perimeter wirelength and 31% reduction in timing violations compared to state-of-the-art analytical placers. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for applying reinforcement learning to electronic design automation, opening promising research directions in self-optimizing physical design tools.

High-level synthesis has emerged as a critical enabling technology for design productivity, yet existing scheduling algorithms exhibit fundamental limitations in handling dynamic resource constraints and communication overhead. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical analysis of an enhanced modulo scheduling framework that integrates precise resource modeling with communication latency awareness. We derive novel theoretical bounds on the initiation interval for conditional dataflow graphs, significantly improving upon classical list scheduling and force-directed scheduling approaches. The key theoretical advancement lies in our formulation of a multi-objective optimization problem that jointly minimizes pipeline latency while respecting area-power constraints in field-programmable systems. We prove that the proposed adaptive scheduling heuristic achieves near-optimal solutions within a provable approximation ratio of 1.5 for general behavior descriptions. Furthermore, we establish theoretical conditions under which the algorithm guarantees convergence to Pareto-optimal schedules. Experimental results on benchmark circuits from the CHStone suite demonstrate that the improved framework reduces average critical path delay by 18% and achieves 12% better resource utilization compared to the state-of-the-art EPIC scheduler, all while maintaining acceptable compilation overhead.

We present SecureSynth, a comprehensive automated design framework for hardware security primitives that fundamentally transforms how cryptographic modules are implemented. Current practice in electronic design automation treats security as a post-synthesis optimization, resulting in suboptimal implementations with exploitable side-channel leakage. SecureSynth introduces a security-aware design flow where threat models and leakage models are co-optimized with traditional design objectives from the earliest stages of electronic system-level design. The system architecture encompasses three core components: a formal specification module supporting privacy-preserving cryptographic protocols, an automatic security constraint extraction engine that analyzes vulnerability profiles, and a leakage-aware synthesis kernel generating protected RTL implementations. Our framework employs a novel leakage quantification metric based on mutual information analysis to guide automatic countermeasure insertion. The design flow has been implemented as an open-source toolchain integrated with standard EDA toolflows. Comprehensive evaluation across 15 cryptographic benchmarks from the cryptography library demonstrates that SecureSynth achieves a 40% reduction in information leakage while maintaining only 8% area overhead compared to unprotected implementations. This work represents the first complete automated framework for hardware security from specification to verified implementation.

This paper introduces VeriCore-X, a substantially enhanced simulation and verification platform for system-on-chip designs that addresses critical scalability and coverage bottlenecks in contemporary hardware verification workflows. The proposed system integrates parallel RTL simulation acceleration, intelligent test generation guided by mutation analysis, and automated formal property checking into a unified verification environment. Key architectural innovations include a distributed simulation engine with dynamic load balancing across heterogeneous compute resources and a machine learning-driven test prioritization mechanism that predicts code coverage hotspots. We developed a novel coverage-directed stimulus generation algorithm that leverages deep reinforcement learning to automatically produce corner-case test scenarios that traditional constrained random verification misses. The complete verification platform has been deployed in an industrial setting and validated on production designs exceeding 50 million gate equivalents. Comparative evaluation against leading commercial verification tools demonstrates that VeriCore-X achieves a 3.2x improvement in verification throughput, identifies 27% more design bugs during the pre-silicon phase, and reduces overall verification cycle time by 45%. The system achieves 94% functional coverage on complex industrial designs with significantly reduced human intervention.
